result.reason: The passage is the opening mishna of perek 12, presenting the basic case of a man who marries a woman and stipulates to support her daughter for five years — exactly what heading 0 ('Perek 12 Opening') introduces as the first mishna of the new chapter, before the detailed analysis begins in heading 1.

The passage describes the remarriage scenario and the second husband's obligation to sustain the daughter for five years, which directly matches the 'Remarriage & Dual Support' section's prose about the second husband's independent five-year obligation.

The passage directly discusses the prohibition on the two husbands combining their obligations and the requirement that one provides food while the other pays the monetary equivalent, which is precisely what the prose under 'Independent Obligations' describes.

The passage covers both the married-daughter scenario and the post-death estate ranking (liened vs. unencumbered property, creditor status), but the bulk of the content — the death of the stepfathers, natural daughters limited to unsold property, and stepdaughter collecting from liened property as a creditor — is precisely what candidate 1 ('After Stepfather Death') discusses in its prose.
The passage directly quotes the 'smart people's clause' about conditioning sustenance on the marriage's continuation, which is exactly what the prose under heading 0 discusses.
The passage contains exactly the opening dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish about oral admission, which is precisely what the 'Oral Admission Debate' section prose describes.

Both items are the core question-and-answer exchange about the disputed case (informal written admission without 'atem eidai'), which is precisely what candidate 0's prose describes in detail — the alima/lo alima milta d'shtara debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

The passage presents the Gemara's challenge using the mishna about sustaining a daughter for five years and asks 'mai lav ki hai gavna' — is this not a case like the informal written admission — which is precisely what the prose of heading 0 ('Written vs Oral') describes and analyzes.

Both items together constitute the gemara's rejection of the prior reading and its substitution of the 'stipulation documents' explanation, which is precisely what the 'Wedding Stipulations' prose describes — the gemara declining the earlier reading and proposing bishtarei psikta as the mishnah's subject, with the Rav Giddel teaching serving as the illustration of that category, all of which the 'Wedding Stipulations' section explicitly introduces before the 'In-Law Negotiations' section elaborates on it.

All three items constitute the complete tashma challenge and its resolution regarding the pidyon haben case — the challenge itself (item 1), the answer about the pre-existing Torah obligation and why the IOU was written (item 2), and Ulla's gezeirah explanation for why the son remains unredeemed (item 3) — which matches the 'Pidyon Haben Case' prose exactly, while candidate 1's prose already describes all this content as its own discussion, suggesting the passage was misplaced one heading too late.

The passage directly introduces Rava's 'k'tana'ei' statement about the guarantor appearing after signatures collecting only from unsold property, which is precisely what the 'Guarantor Dispute' section's prose describes and discusses.
Both items together form the Ben Nanas dispute and strangling parable that candidate 0's prose explicitly and fully discusses, matching the content precisely.

All three items discuss the mapping of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish onto Rabbi Yishmael and Ben Nanas, and the refinement that the dispute only applies according to Rabbi Yishmael — exactly what the 'Yochanan vs Resh Lakish' prose describes.

All three items discuss the same topic — Rav Giddel's ruling about verbal obligations becoming binding through kiddushin, and Rava's elaboration on the mechanism of hana'ah d'kamichtani ahadadi — which precisely matches the prose of heading 0 about kinyan amira and the joy of the children's marriage serving as consideration.

All three items form one continuous exchange between Ravina and Rav Ashi about whether verbal stipulations can be written down, including the challenge from 'hapikhin hayu kotvin' and the resolution that 'kotvin' means 'omrin' — exactly what candidate 1 ('No Retroactive Writing') describes in its prose.

The passage directly presents the challenge from the mishna about writing betrothal/marriage documents and asks whether it refers to shtarei psikta, which is precisely what the prose under 'Shtar Kiddushin Rules' (index 0) discusses.

The passage directly presents the dispute between Rabbah/Ravina and Rav Pappa/Rav Sherevya about writing a betrothal document without the woman's consent, which is precisely what the 'Unilateral Writing Debate' prose describes.

The passage presents the mishna's statement that the stepdaughter is sustained from liened property because she is like a creditor — this is the content described in the 'Stepdaughter as Creditor' prose, not the 'Implicit Shtar Question' prose which discusses the inference drawn from that fact.

All five items trace the gemara's chain of kinyan/shtar reasoning — from 'beshekanu miyado' through the kegon d'girshah v'ahadrah objection to the final 'leisa b'tnai beit din' resolution — which is precisely what the 'Not Standard Obligation' prose describes in detail.

The passage directly explains the 'eima tzerorei apistinhu' reasoning — that natural daughters don't collect from liened property because the stipulation of the court creates a presumption that the father already gave them funds — which is precisely what the 'Presumption for Daughters' prose discusses.
